content.title: Simplifying and Operating with Square Roots
content.overview: This lesson focuses on simplifying square-root expressions by extracting perfect-square factors and combining like radicals through addition, subtraction, and multiplication.
learning_objectives: Identify and extract perfect-square factors from radicands.
Simplify radical terms into the form k√b.
Combine like radicals by performing arithmetic on their coefficients.
Multiply square-root expressions and simplify the resulting product.

sections.title: Simplifying a Single Radical
sections.content: To simplify a square root, look for the largest perfect-square factor (e.g., 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) within the radicand (the number under the symbol). Use the property √ab = √a · √b. If 'a' is a perfect square, you can take its square root outside the radical. For example, √75 = √(25 · 3) = √25 · √3 = 5√3.

sections.title: Adding and Subtracting Like Radicals
sections.content:
Radicals are 'like' only if they have the exact same radicand. You can combine like radicals by adding or subtracting their outside coefficients, similar to combining like terms in algebra (e.g., 3x + 2x = 5x). If the radicands are different, you must simplify them first to see if they can be matched. For example, 5√2 + 3√2 = 8√2, but 5√2 + 3√3 cannot be combined further.

![A flowchart showing the process: Factor Radicands, Extract Perfect Squares, Multiply by Coefficients, Combine Like Radicals.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/724450c9-c465-4ff3-8353-8f9bbba50046-1786505491933-850.webp)

sections.title: Multiplying Radicals
sections.content: When multiplying square roots, use the rule (a√b) · (c√d) = (ac)√(bd). Multiply the coefficients outside the radicals together, and multiply the radicands inside the radicals together. After multiplying, always check if the new radicand can be simplified further by extracting perfect squares.

worked_examples.question: Simplify the expression: 3√8 + 2√18 - √32
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Factor each radicand to find perfect squares. √8 = √(4·2) = 2√2. √18 = √(9·2) = 3√2. √32 = √(16·2) = 4√2. Step 2: Multiply by the original coefficients. 3(2√2) = 6√2. 2(3√2) = 6√2. -1(4√2) = -4√2. Step 3: Combine the like radicals. (6 + 6 - 4)√2 = 8√2.

worked_examples.question: Find the product: (2√5) · (4√10)
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply the outside coefficients: 2 · 4 = 8. Step 2: Multiply the radicands: √5 · √10 = √50. Step 3: Combine results: 8√50. Step 4: Simplify the radical. √50 = √(25·2) = 5√2. Step 5: Final multiplication: 8 · 5√2 = 40√2.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the extracted square root by the existing coefficient outside the radical.
Failing to simplify the radicand completely (e.g., leaving √48 instead of 4√3).
Treating √8 as 4√2 instead of 2√2 (confusing the factor with its square root).
exam_tips: Memorize perfect squares up to 144 to quickly identify factors.
If you are stuck on a radical addition problem, simplify every term first; they will almost always result in the same radicand.
Use your calculator to check work: decimal approximations of the original expression and your simplified answer should match.
content.recap: To master square roots, factor out perfect squares to simplify each term, combine only those terms with identical radicands by adjusting their coefficients, and multiply both inside and outside values when finding products.

knowledge_claims.content: The radicand is the value located inside the square root symbol.
The product property of radicals states that √a · √b = √(ab) for all non-negative real numbers.
To simplify a radical, factor the radicand into a product containing the largest possible perfect square, then take the square root of that factor outside the radical.
Like radicals are terms that have the exact same radicand after being fully simplified.
When adding or subtracting like radicals, only the coefficients are combined; the radicand remains unchanged.
It is a common error to add radicands together, such as claiming √a + √b = √(a+b), which is mathematically incorrect.
When a radical is simplified and moved outside, it must be multiplied by any existing coefficient already present in front of the radical.
The expression √32 simplifies to 4√2 because 32 is the product of the perfect square 16 and 2.
The expression 3√5 + 2√5 simplifies to 5√5 by adding the coefficients 3 and 2.
To multiply (x√y) and (w√z), calculate (x·w)√(y·z) and then simplify the resulting radical.
A radical is fully simplified only when the radicand contains no factors that are perfect squares other than 1.
Unlike variables in algebra, radicals with different radicands cannot be combined into a single radical term through addition or subtraction.
